question: What do we call a disease that is always present at a steady, expected level in a specific community?
explanation: You've got this! An endemic disease hangs around at a predictable, steady level in a specific area—like malaria in many parts of Nigeria—without causing sudden panic. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T76#GNS214_U1_T76_h1)

question: How is an epidemic different from an endemic disease?

options.A: An endemic illness only appears once every ten years in a community.
options.B: An epidemic represents a sudden spike in cases above the normal expected baseline.
options.C: An endemic condition spreads much faster than any known epidemic.
options.D: An epidemic only affects people living in cold weather climates.

explanation: Great thinking! While an endemic disease is steady and expected, an epidemic breaks that baseline with an unusual, sudden surge of new cases. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T76#GNS214_U1_T76_h1)

question: What are the three core parts of the epidemiological triad used to study diseases?
explanation: Spot on! The epidemiological triad looks at the interacting relationship between the agent, the host, and their environment to understand how diseases spread. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T76#GNS214_U1_T76_h2)

question: If you notice stagnant water sitting outside a house, which part of the epidemiological triad does this represent?
explanation: Well done! Stagnant water is an external physical condition around us that helps mosquitoes breed, making it an environmental factor. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T76#GNS214_U1_T76_h2)

question: What is the main goal of disease surveillance in public health?

options.A: To ensure that hospitals charge the correct fees for admissions
options.B: To punish clinics that fail to treat enough patients each month
options.C: To test new pharmaceutical drugs on healthy volunteer populations
options.D: To collect and analyze health data for early detection and planning

explanation: Exactly! Surveillance is like a early-warning radar. It tracks disease patterns continuously so health workers can spot trouble and plan ahead. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T76#GNS214_U1_T76_h3)

question: A clinic nurse notices an unusual rise in severe watery diarrhea cases over two days. What should she do first?

options.A: Wait another month to see if the patient numbers drop on their own
options.B: Prescribe strong antibiotics to everyone living in the local village
options.C: Close the clinic permanently to prevent any further infections
options.D: Report the unusual cluster to public health authorities for investigation

explanation: You nailed it! Catching unusual symptom clusters early and reporting them helps stop outbreaks like cholera right in their tracks. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T76#GNS214_U1_T76_h3)

question: In infectious disease, what exactly is a 'vector'?

options.A: A chemical spray used to clean operating theatre floors
options.B: An inanimate object like a door handle that carries bacteria
options.C: A specialized blood test used to diagnose viral infections
options.D: A living organism that transmits a pathogen from one host to another

explanation: Think of mosquitoes or ticks! Vectors are living creatures that carry germs from one person or animal to another. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T76#GNS214_U1_T76_h4)

question: Which of these actions is an example of environmental source reduction to prevent malaria?

options.A: Taking daily anti-malarial tablets prescribed by a doctor
options.B: Draining stagnant puddles of water around the residential compound
options.C: Treating infected patients with intravenous fluid therapy
options.D: Getting vaccinated against mosquito-borne viral infections

explanation: Spot on! Source reduction is about removing the breeding grounds—like clearing out stagnant water where mosquitoes love to lay eggs. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T76#GNS214_U1_T76_h4)

question: What is the main purpose of herd immunity in a community?

options.A: To cure individuals who already show advanced symptoms of illness
options.B: To protect vulnerable people by making most of the community immune
options.C: To completely eliminate all known bacteria from the human gut
options.D: To ensure every citizen takes a daily dose of vitamin supplements

explanation: Great job! When most people are immune (usually through vaccination), the germ struggles to find anyone new to infect, shielding the most vulnerable among us. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T76#GNS214_U1_T76_h5)

question: How does chemoprophylaxis differ from standard immunization?

options.A: Chemoprophylaxis cures chronic illnesses, while immunization is only used for acute emergency surgeries.
options.B: Chemoprophylaxis creates lifelong immunity, whereas vaccines wear off after a single week.
options.C: Immunization is given to animals only, whereas chemoprophylaxis is exclusively reserved for human patients.
options.D: Chemoprophylaxis uses medications to prevent infection, whereas immunization uses antigens to stimulate antibody production.

explanation: You've got this! Chemoprophylaxis means using protective drugs (like malaria prevention tablets), while vaccines train your body's own immune system to fight back. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T76#GNS214_U1_T76_h5)

question: What is usually the very first formal step when investigating a suspected disease outbreak?

options.A: Burn all personal belongings of infected residents
options.B: Verify the clinical diagnosis through laboratory testing
options.C: Construct a brand new tertiary care hospital

explanation: Before jumping to conclusions or panicking, public health teams must first confirm through lab tests that the suspected germ is actually there. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T76#GNS214_U1_T76_h6)

question: Why is having a clear 'case definition' so important when investigating an outbreak?

options.A: It guarantees that pharmaceutical companies will donate free drugs to the clinic.
options.B: It stops the infectious agent from mutating into a more dangerous strain.
options.C: It ensures all healthcare workers use the exact same criteria to count and track cases.
options.D: It allows nurses to diagnose patients without needing any formal medical training.

explanation: Brilliant! A clear case definition makes sure everyone is on the same page about what symptoms count, preventing messy or inaccurate data tracking. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T76#GNS214_U1_T76_h6)

question: Why is it so helpful to involve local community leaders in public health campaigns?

options.A: It builds trust and encourages residents to adopt healthy behaviors.
options.B: It allows the government to avoid spending money on medical supplies.
options.C: It guarantees that no one in the village will ever catch a virus.
options.D: It removes the need for nurses to provide direct patient care.

explanation: You're right! Local leaders have the community's trust. When they support a health initiative, people are much more likely to listen and join in. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T76#GNS214_U1_T76_h7)

question: A nurse is teaching a rural community about cholera prevention. Which approach will work best?

options.A: Insisting that villagers change their ancient cultural practices without any explanation
options.B: Handing out complex scientific research journals written in advanced medical terminology
options.C: Waiting until an outbreak kills several people before holding a public meeting
options.D: Using local languages and culturally relevant examples to explain safe drinking water habits

explanation: Spot on! Keeping health education simple, friendly, and in the local language ensures everyone understands and can easily protect themselves. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T76#GNS214_U1_T76_h7)
